position: Port the backend to Java 21 / Spring Boot behind the existing React front end, keep Bunny, keep Postgres. Do it as a strangler over four slices, not a rewrite: the React UI (13,326 lines, 59 of 70 components already 'use client') and the media pipeline are the two most expensive assets in the repository and neither is the thing that hurts. What hurts is a 1,869-line untested production database driver, a scheduler that turns itself off, and per-process state pretending to be global — and all three are artefacts of running a stateful product on a stateless serverless runtime, which is exactly what a long-lived JVM stops being true.
summary: Sandeep does not have an unmanageable repository; he has a manageable repository running on the wrong execution model. Every real=true finding from the four code reviews that is structural rather than cosmetic traces to one of three serverless consequences: there is no long-lived process, so rate limits and health memos live in one instance's memory (lib/http/rate-limit.ts:16, lib/health/probes.ts:28) and lockouts are N times looser than their stated numbers; there is no in-process scheduler, so four of six cron jobs ride a public repo's GitHub Actions workflow that GitHub disables after 60 days of no commits (.github/workflows/notify-drain.yml:14-15) because Vercel's plan allows exactly two (vercel.json:9-18, app/api/cron/notify/route.ts:18-21); and there is no ambient database in the test environment, so a second in-memory driver was written to make the suite runnable (lib/db/repository.ts:29-39) and has now drifted from the production driver badly enough that unpublished photographs are served to guests today (lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1625-1631 accepts no liveOnly option at all, against lib/db/repository.ts:343 which declares it, and lib/db/memory-repository.ts:746-757 which implements it correctly). A JVM makes all three go away by construction rather than by discipline: @Scheduled with a Postgres advisory lock, a shared Caffeine/Redis bucket, and Testcontainers, which makes 'the tests run against the real Postgres' the default instead of an aspiration nobody funds. Go buys the same three properties; Java buys them plus the largest engineering hiring pool in India, which is the only reason to prefer it over Go, and it is a sufficient reason for a founder whose bus factor is currently one. The honest price is 18 engineer-months, roughly 11 calendar months at two engineers, about ₹11,500/month of new infrastructure, the loss of 659 tests and of the one-folder-per-module contract that is this codebase's best idea, and zero help with a grant application. Nobody should do this at 6 orgs and 5 catalogues pre-revenue. It becomes correct the day a second engineer is hired or the first enterprise diligence asks who else can run this.
architecture:
Four slices, each independently shippable and independently reversible, with the Next.js app staying in front the whole way.

Slice 0 — the seam already exists and is the reason this is a port and not a rewrite. lib/db/repository.ts is a 103-method interface with two implementations; lib/video/provider.ts is a five-method interface whose own header says switching providers is 'a new implementation of this interface and one line in lib/video/index.ts'. Those two files are the contract a Spring service has to satisfy. The 24 SQL migrations in supabase/migrations/ move to Flyway unchanged — the same Postgres, the same tables, no data migration, no dual-write, no backfill. That is the single biggest cost this option avoids relative to a full rebuild: the database does not move.

Slice 1 — jobs and the pipeline (the part with no UI, and the part that is actually broken). Spring Boot service, @Scheduled for all six jobs currently split across vercel.json and two GitHub Actions workflows, a Postgres advisory lock so two instances do not double-drain. The notification queue drain becomes SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, which is precisely the 'claim a row before sending' fix that N-54 is paused on because Next's serverless shape makes it awkward. The Bunny webhook receiver (HMAC, lib/video/bunny.ts:264-305), the TUS ticket signer (:74-93), the directory-scoped playback token (:96-148) and the reconcile poller port method-for-method. Bunny does not change, so nothing about upload, transcode or delivery is at risk in this slice. Nothing user-facing moves; Next keeps serving every page.

Slice 2 — the guest hot path. lib/catalogue-access.ts is 88 lines and one function with six verdicts (missing/draft/locked/lapsed/premiere/ok, resolved in that exact order at :30-66). It becomes a Spring @Service plus a Caffeine cache, exposed as one endpoint the Next guest page calls, and the playback-token endpoint moves with it. The 10-second progress heartbeat (components/streaming/useProgressHeartbeat.ts:5) stops being a cold serverless function making six PostgREST round trips per beat (app/api/progress/route.ts:38-73) and becomes a pooled JDBC write with an in-memory coalescer — this is the one place where the JVM is not just tidier but materially cheaper per request. Note honestly that the guest page is already dynamic on every render (app/c/[slug]/page.tsx:21 declares revalidate=3600 but lib/guest-locale.ts:22-23 calls cookies() unconditionally and the page awaits searchParams), so nothing static is being given up here; the ISR the scale plan assumes does not exist today either way.

Slice 3 — admin writes. All 60 API routes under app/api/ become Spring MVC controllers. lib/admin/session.ts's three guards (requireOperator / requireOwnedCatalogue / requireEditableCatalogue) become a single @OrgScoped annotation on a Spring Security method interceptor plus an ArchUnit test asserting every controller method under /api/admin carries it — which converts the one rule CLAUDE.md names as 'where the risk actually is' from a convention into a build failure. That is the conversion the maintainability review asked for and the TypeScript codebase has no clean way to express.

Slice 4 — the 26 server components. This is the slice everyone underestimates. 26 of 40 page.tsx files read the repository directly inside a React Server Component (app/admin/platform/page.tsx, app/admin/c/[id]/customizer/page.tsx, app/my/page.tsx and 23 others). They are not front end; they are backend reads that happen to render. Each needs a Java read endpoint and either a client fetch with a loading state or a Next BFF fetch. Two defensible shapes: (a) Next stays as a thin BFF, keeps server rendering, and calls Java over HTTP on a private network — one extra hop, no UI rewrite; or (b) those pages go client-rendered like the other 59 components already are, and Next becomes almost static. Recommend (a) for the guest surface where the 1.5-second budget lives, (b) for the admin console where a spinner is acceptable. Do not let this slice be decided implicitly.

What stays untouched: Bunny Stream and Storage; all 24 migrations and the Postgres schema; every one of the 59 'use client' components and all 9 module Guest/Editor components; the customizer's live preview, which CLAUDE.md protects as deliberate deviation #1 and which survives intact because it is pure React mounting real guest components; Tailwind v4 and the seven-theme CSS-custom-property system (themes/, 382 lines) which never touches a server; the 16 Playwright E2E specs, which drive a browser and do not care what language answers.

What has to be split in two: modules/. Today a module is one folder — modules/billboard/index.ts is 70 lines carrying meta, a Zod schema, Guest, a lazily-imported Editor, defaults(), consumes() and advise() together. Java must own config validation (it is a server trust boundary) while React owns rendering, so that folder becomes a Java record plus a TS folder plus a generated contract between them. Generate the TypeScript types from the Java schema, never hand-maintain both. This is the real architectural loss and it should be named out loud, not discovered in month four.
benefits: Kills the one finding both the maintainability and scalability reviews rated high, structurally rather than by fixing a line. Today lib/db/supabase-repository.ts is 1,869 lines that no test ever executes — every unit test instantiates MemoryRepository directly, and the single integration test that touches listTitles({publishedOnly:true}) is gated behind RUN_INTEGRATION=1, outside pnpm verify and outside CI. The drivers have already diverged: Supabase filters on published and status but never live_at (:1390-1396), and listPhotosForCatalogue does not even accept the liveOnly option lib/db/repository.ts:343 declares (:1625-1631), so every photograph is visible to guests the instant the upload finishes, before Publish, in production, right now. In Java with Testcontainers, a real Postgres in the test suite is the default posture, the second driver has no reason to exist, and this entire class of bug becomes impossible — not unlikely, impossible, because there is only one implementation and the tests run it.

Ends the scheduler-that-disables-itself problem. Four of six jobs (notify, lifecycle, warnings, synthetic) run from .github/workflows/notify-drain.yml and synthetic-check.yml because Vercel's plan allows exactly two crons (vercel.json:9-18, reason given in app/api/cron/notify/route.ts:18-21). GitHub disables a public repo's scheduled workflows after 60 days without a commit, and both workflow files say so in their own headers. For a product where a quiet month is entirely plausible, the consequence is that every queued email silently stops sending, the lapse ladder stops walking, expiry warnings stop queueing and the synthetic guest-path check stops alerting, with only a GitHub email as warning. A Spring @Scheduled method in a process that is always running has no such property, and there is no two-cron ceiling to design around.

Makes per-instance state actually global. lib/http/rate-limit.ts:16 and lib/health/probes.ts:28 are plain Maps in one Vercel instance's memory, and the file says so in its own comment. With CAPTCHA_DRIVER=none in production, that approximate limiter is the only thing between a script and a four-digit passcode, a password guess, or a credential-link brute force. In a JVM the same call sites back onto one shared bucket with no call-site change; with two instances behind a load balancer, one Redis line. The health-probe memo and the domains page stop disagreeing for up to a minute (lib/health/probes.ts:208-226 vs app/admin/platform/domains/page.tsx:20-24).

Turns the org-scoping invariant into a compiler-and-build problem. CLAUDE.md names lib/admin/session.ts as 'the only place org_id enters a query' and the maintainability review confirms the discipline currently holds perfectly across 34 admin route files and 46 handlers — with no automated check whatsoever. Spring Security method interception plus one ArchUnit rule makes a route that forgets the guard fail the build. That is the difference between a rule the founder remembers and a rule the repository enforces, and it is the single most valuable thing to pin before a second engineer touches this code.

Makes the heartbeat and the nightly rollup cheap and interruptible. The progress heartbeat fires every 10 seconds per watching guest (useProgressHeartbeat.ts:5) into a force-dynamic route that makes getProfile, getTitle, getProgress, upsertProgress, recordPlayEvent and sometimes updateTitle — six PostgREST round trips per beat, each a fresh HTTP connection from a cold-ish function. A pooled JDBC connection with a write coalescer collapses that to one batched statement per beat or per ten. Separately, app/api/cron/usage/route.ts:51-69 walks every catalogue × every title serially with one provider call each, no maxDuration and no resume; a JVM job with a thread pool, a checkpoint and a real timeout is the ordinary shape of that work rather than a race against a function limit.

Fixes the migration story as a side effect. There is no migration ledger today — docs/DEPLOYMENT.md:116 says outright that which migrations are applied 'is a question the tables answer', and all 24 go into production by pasting SQL into a web console. Flyway comes free with the Spring starter, makes the ledger a table, makes the applier a CLI, and makes a schema change part of the deploy rather than a manual step before it.

Hiring, which is the actual argument and the reason to prefer Java over Go. Java/Spring is by a wide margin the deepest backend hiring pool in India at every seniority and price point; a competent Spring engineer in Bengaluru or Pune can be productive on a Spring Boot service in a week. The pool for 'Next.js App Router with React Server Components, Zod, and a hand-rolled repository seam' is a fraction of that size and skews expensive and remote. Today Mehfilbox is 179 commits by one author plus an agent, which means the bus factor is one; every recovery plan that depends on hiring runs through this constraint. Go's pool in India is real but perhaps a fifth the size, and much more concentrated in infrastructure companies than in product teams.

Keeps the two decisions that the evidence says are already right. Bunny stays, and the cost model is unambiguous that it should: ₹7,534/month at 10 weddings versus ₹19,971 infra-only self-hosted (₹54,971 including people), and still cheaper at 60 weddings (₹45,207 vs ₹54,508) and at 300 (₹2.26L vs ₹2.49L). React stays, and 59 of the 70 files in components/ already carry 'use client', so the front end is very nearly an SPA that happens to be served by Next — keeping it costs almost nothing and rewriting it would cost more than the backend.
costs_and_losses: 659 tests across 66 unit and component files (9,312 lines) are the repository's only repeatable proof that it works, and the majority of them — everything that exercises lib/ logic against MemoryRepository — do not port. They get rewritten in JUnit against Testcontainers. Budget two full engineer-months for this and expect the rewritten suite to be smaller and to miss things the original caught, for at least a quarter. During that quarter the product is less safe than it is today, which is the opposite of the reason for doing the port.

The one-folder module contract dies. modules/billboard/index.ts is 70 lines holding schema, Guest, Editor, defaults, consumes and advise in one place, and tests/unit/registry.test.ts enforces that no file outside modules/ ever names a module type. Split across Java and TypeScript, that test cannot span the boundary, adding a module goes from 'one folder plus one registry line' (the whole premise of .claude/skills/add-module) to a Java record plus a TS folder plus a generated contract, and advise()'s copywriting-adjacent logic either duplicates or moves away from the component it describes. This is the best idea in the codebase and the port damages it.

MemoryRepository (1,096 lines) and with it the offline demo. CLAUDE.md's deliberate deviation #2 exists so the suite, CI and a planner demo run with no database. Testcontainers is a good trade for CI but it needs Docker, and the 'open a laptop with no network and show a planner a working catalogue' capability has to be rebuilt or abandoned. Decide which, in writing, before slice 1.

26 of 40 pages lose zero-round-trip data access. Every page.tsx under app/admin/platform/, app/admin/c/[id]/, app/admin/studio/ and app/my/ reads the repository inside a server component today. Each one gains a network hop, a loading state, an error state and a serialisation boundary. This is the least glamorous slice, the easiest to under-scope, and the one most likely to make the admin console feel slower after the port than before it.

Two systems live at once for the whole cutover. The four real=true defects — the driver drift, the self-disabling scheduler, the per-instance lockouts, the absent staging environment — must be fixed in the TypeScript codebase anyway, because guests are being served wrongly today and the port lands in month eleven. So you pay for those fixes twice: once as patches to code you are deleting, once as properties of the code replacing it. Budget half an engineer-month for the throwaway fixes and do not skip them.

Roughly ₹11,500/month of new infrastructure and about ₹1.4 lakh a year, moving modelled infra from ~17% of revenue at 60 weddings to somewhere near 20–21%. Today the platform side is about ₹4,300/month (Vercel Pro $20 + Supabase Pro $25 at ₹95.7/USD). A two-instance JVM deployment in an Indian region is roughly: 2 × small ARM app instance ₹4,700, load balancer ₹1,900, log and metric retention ₹2,800 (a thing there is none of today — N-53b), Redis or an equivalent for shared buckets ₹1,150, registry and egress ₹950, plus the Vercel and Supabase lines that do not go away because the front end and the database both stay. Call it ₹15,800/month for the platform and ₹23,300 all-in at 10 weddings/month with Bunny's ₹7,534. Instance prices for a Mumbai region are estimates and should be quoted before anyone commits; the Bunny and FX figures come from the measured cost model.

Eleven months of no new product. Razorpay does not exist — not one line of payment code, no webhook, no invoice table, no RAZORPAY_* variable anywhere (map-commerce §7.1-2). A pre-revenue product with no payment path spending a year changing the language its backend is written in is spending its runway on an internal quality it can currently only assert, not sell.

Java is more verbose and the agent leverage drops. The throughput that produced this repository — 179 commits in five weeks, one author plus an agent — comes substantially from one strictly-typed language with colocated tests where a single change fits in one context window. Two languages with a generated contract between them means every cross-cutting change is two edits in two repositories with a codegen step in the middle. Expect less from the agent per session, not more.

Type-level expressiveness is lost in places that matter. lib/catalogue-access.ts's AccessVerdict is a discriminated union of six variants and requireServableCatalogue switches on it exhaustively — the TypeScript compiler proves no case is missed. Java 21's sealed interfaces plus pattern-matching switch give the same guarantee, so this particular one survives; but the ~20 Zod schemas in lib/schema.ts (690 lines) that parse, coerce, default and refine in one declaration become Jakarta Bean Validation annotations plus explicit mapping code, and the field-to-column maps the maintainability review already flags as untested get longer, not shorter.
risks: The Bunny webhook is the highest-consequence moving part and this repository cannot see it. It is a manual dashboard setting no code here can read, verify or change (docs/DEPLOYMENT.md:58-68), pnpm preflight checks every other Bunny setting but not this one, and it has already caused one real incident — the second-pass domain switchover left it pointed at the old alias and docs/GO-LIVE.md:213-244 calls it 'the trap… a webhook that looks healthy is the hardest kind to debug', because uploads succeed, transcoding finishes, and titles simply never leave processing. A cutover doubles the number of hosts it could be pointed at and there is no automated check to catch a wrong one. Mitigation: repoint it exactly once, in slice 1, with a real film uploaded and watched to ready, and add a webhook-liveness probe to the Java service on day one.

There is no staging environment to port into. N-87 (docs/NEXT.md:181-194) is labelled 'debt that is costing us': Vercel Preview has zero variables, lib/env.ts refuses a production build on an ephemeral driver, CI pins DATA_DRIVER=memory and VIDEO_DRIVER=fake for every job including E2E, and scripts/deploy-vercel.sh:27 defaults TARGET to production. Today a migration and the build that needs it meet for the first time in production. Doing an eleven-month backend port into that is the single largest process risk in this plan and it must be fixed before slice 1, not during it.

The port is a bet that a second engineer arrives. If the hire does not happen, Sandeep has traded a codebase he is fluent in for one he is re-learning, in a language whose main advantage — the hiring pool — he is not using. This risk is not hedged by anything in the plan; it is the plan's premise. If the answer to 'am I hiring a backend engineer in the next two quarters' is no or maybe, the correct decision is to not start.

Estimate risk on the 26 server components. Eighteen engineer-months assumes slice 4 takes two. If the admin console turns out to need real loading and error states everywhere rather than a BFF passthrough, that slice alone can be four, and 18 becomes 20-22. The honest range is 14 to 22 engineer-months and the wide end is more likely than the narrow one.

Feature freeze discipline. A strangler port only works if the TypeScript side stops growing. Eleven months is long enough that a studio will ask for something, and every feature added mid-port is built twice. There is no technical mitigation, only a written rule and the willingness to say no to a customer in a pre-revenue business — which is exactly when it is hardest.

A dual-stack runtime has failure modes neither stack has alone: a Next BFF timing out on a Java call it used to make in-process, a session cookie signed by one and read by the other, CORS and cookie-domain mistakes on the guest path. Note that SESSION_SECRET is currently overloaded three ways (operator sessions and passcode grants via lib/auth.ts:26, fake-driver playback tokens and the fake webhook signature via lib/video/fake.ts:61 and :131, and the cron bearer fallback in all six cron routes) with no documented rotation path — that secret has to be untangled before two runtimes share it, not after.

Java's default answers are heavier than this product needs. A Spring team's instinct is JPA, a service layer, a DTO layer and a mapper layer, and the result is more code than the 10,940 lines of lib/ it replaces, not less. If the point of the exercise is that the repository feels unmanageable, a naive Spring port makes it worse. Mandate jOOQ or Spring Data JDBC over JPA, records over beans, and one package per subsystem mirroring the nine maps — or the port delivers the hiring benefit and loses the comprehensibility one.
what_it_does_not_fix: The documentation, which is where the review found the most findings. Five competing entry points, two contradicting each other on reading order; docs/GO-LIVE.md three stacked runbooks under a retired domain's title; docs/PRODUCT.md §1.1 and the notification rows describing a product two phases behind what shipped; four unsynchronised files carrying live-looking ₹ prices against zero prices in code; an API contract covering 13 of 60 routes. None of that is a language problem and a port changes none of it. It also invalidates docs/spec/, CLAUDE.md, all four .claude/skills/ and the entire agent runbook on the day slice 1 lands.

The missing product. Razorpay is entirely absent, plans is a table with zero rows and no reader, catalogue-level entitlements are dead code no route can reach, storage quota is the only entitlement lever that works, and what PRICING.md sells (100-200 GB) is not what the code enforces (a flat 20 GB). The theme store Sandeep is considering has no owner column, no price, no entitlement check, no versioning and no third-party author role. A Java backend ships none of this, and eleven months of porting is eleven months of not shipping it.

Grants and diligence — be blunt about this. DPIIT recognition is free self-certification against an entity test (Pvt Ltd / LLP / partnership / cooperative, under 10 years, under ₹200 crore turnover) and an innovation sentence; nothing in the process asks what language the backend is written in. SISFS scores eight criteria set by the incubator — market need, feasibility, potential impact, novelty and IP, team strength, fund-utilisation plan — and requires incorporation within 2 years, ≥51% Indian promoter shareholding and ≤₹10 lakh of prior government support. 'We rewrote the backend in Java' scores zero on all eight and actively hurts one: a milestone-based ₹20 lakh grant is disbursed against proof-of-concept and product-trial milestones, and an internal port produces no milestone an ISMC can recognise. The two honest, marginal points in its favour: SISFS §7.2 scores feasibility partly on team strength, and 'a stack we can hire for in India' is a better answer than 'a stack one person knows'; and a Series-A technical diligence will eventually ask about bus factor, single-driver test coverage and who else can operate this. Neither is worth eleven months on its own. What actually helps the grant narrative is incorporating the Pvt Ltd within the 2-year SISFS window and having a paying customer — and the port delays the second.
The cost structure. Bunny stays, correctly, and it is the largest infrastructure line at every scale modelled. The port adds about ₹11,500/month and removes nothing.

The genuine product defects that are not architectural: single-photo delete reclaiming only the master rendition while catalogue delete loops every width; the 4 MB limit whose refusal message says 25 MB; a film's slug frozen to its upload filename forever (N-84); photographs served unsigned on a public pull zone (N-83); the passcode granting downloads that D-43 says need an account (N-85); the captions and speed controls the spec requires, the data path carries and the player never renders. Every one of these ports across as a bug in a new language unless someone fixes it, and a port is the worst possible moment to be fixing product bugs.

Sandeep's actual complaint. 'The repository feels unmanageable' at 35,000 source lines across 106 pages-and-routes, 70 components, 70 lib files and 9 modules is a navigation and documentation problem, not a size problem — this is a small codebase by any professional standard. A Java port produces more total lines, in two languages, with a generated contract between them. If nothing else in this document persuades, that sentence should: the port is defensible on hiring and on execution model, and indefensible as a cure for the feeling that prompted the question.
triggers_to_revisit: A second engineer is being hired, or is already hired. This is the trigger. If a Spring engineer is starting in the next two quarters, start slice 1 the week before they do and let them own it; if nobody is being hired, none of the rest of this matters.

The GitHub Actions scheduler actually pauses — a 60-day gap in commits, or an email from GitHub saying the workflows are disabled. That is the moment the serverless execution model has visibly cost a customer an email, and the argument stops being theoretical.

Throughput on Vercel's shape starts being the binding constraint: SCALE-PLAN's function-invocation ceiling is modelled at roughly 300 weddings/month, and the 10-second heartbeat is the dominant term. If weddings per month crosses ~100 with the heartbeat unchanged, the JVM's per-request economics stop being a nicety.

The first enterprise or platform customer asks for an on-premise or private-cloud deployment, a data-residency guarantee, or a SOC-2-shaped questionnaire. The Dockerfile that is meant to be the anti-lock-in answer has not been built in CI since 594c5e9 (2026-08-14), predates 18 migrations, and per docs/DEPLOYMENT.md §10 would deploy a product that never drains notifications, never runs the lapse ladder and never queues a warning. A JVM container is a genuine answer to that question; the current one is not.

A second real driver drift ships to production after the Supabase/memory one is fixed. Once is a bug; twice means the two-driver design is structurally unsafe and the test-against-a-real-database posture has to be bought, whatever it costs.

Bunny's economics or availability change — a committed contract that is not competitive, a Mumbai origin that never arrives, or a delivery-terms change. That would reopen the media question, which is a different decision from this one and should be taken on cost.json's numbers, not on language.

A trigger to abandon mid-port, stated in advance so it is not a judgement call later: if slice 1 (jobs and pipeline, estimated 3 engineer-months) has not reached production by month five, stop, keep the Java jobs runner if it works, and put everything else back. Slice 1 is deliberately the slice you can keep in isolation.
migration_path: Month 0, before any Java is written — fix in TypeScript what is broken today, because the port lands in month eleven and guests are being served wrongly now. Add the live_at predicate to SupabaseRepository.listTitles and give listPhotosForCatalogue the liveOnly option it already declares (lib/db/supabase-repository.ts:1390-1396, :1625-1631). Turn on Turnstile. Move the rate-limit buckets behind a table. Re-enable the GitHub schedules and set a calendar reminder. Half an engineer-month, thrown away deliberately.

Month 0-1 — build the staging environment N-87 describes. A second Supabase project, a Vercel preview target with real variables, and a CI job that runs migrations against it. Nothing else in this plan is safe without it, and it is the one piece of work that is valuable whether or not the port ever happens.

Month 1 — freeze the contract. Generate OpenAPI from the 103 Repository methods and the 60 route handlers, check it into the repository, and generate TypeScript clients from it. Every subsequent slice is 'replace the implementation behind this contract', which is what makes each one reversible. Move the 24 SQL files into Flyway against the same database, verify the checksum ledger matches what is already applied, and delete the paste-into-the-console step from the deployment doc.

Months 2-4 — slice 1: jobs, crons, notification drain, Bunny webhook, reconcile, usage rollup, in a Spring Boot service with no user-facing surface. Repoint the Bunny webhook exactly once, upload a real film, watch it reach ready. Run the Java jobs and the GitHub Actions jobs in parallel for two weeks with the Java side writing to a shadow table, diff the outputs, then cut over. This slice is independently valuable: even if the port stops here, the self-disabling-scheduler problem is solved.

Months 4-6 — slice 2: the guest hot path. Port lib/catalogue-access.ts's six-verdict function and the playback-token endpoint, with the Java service behind the Next guest page. Instrument against the 1.5-second start budget before and after — if the extra hop costs more than 150ms at p75 on 4G, keep the verdict in Next and port only the heartbeat. The heartbeat is the piece with the clearest payoff; take it first within the slice.

Months 6-9 — slice 3: the 60 admin API routes, controller by controller, with the @OrgScoped annotation and the ArchUnit rule in place from the first controller. Run the 16 Playwright E2E specs against every intermediate state — they drive a browser and do not care which runtime answers, which makes them the integration test for the whole cutover. Keep both implementations live behind a per-route flag so any single route can be reverted in one deploy.

Months 9-11 — slice 4: the 26 server-rendered pages. Guest surface keeps Next as a BFF; admin console goes client-rendered. Split the module contract last, when everything else is stable: Java records own validation, the Java schema generates the TypeScript types, modules/ keeps Guest and Editor, and add-module's skill doc is rewritten the same week rather than left stale.

Month 11 — decommission. Delete MemoryRepository and the ephemeral-driver machinery, or decide explicitly to keep the offline demo and say how. Rewrite CLAUDE.md, docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, the four skills and docs/spec/13-agent-runbook.md's reading map on the same day the last route moves, because a port whose documentation lags is how a codebase starts feeling unmanageable in the first place.

Grant scoring, from the researched primary sources: DPIIT recognition requires only an eligible entity type, age under 10 years, turnover under ₹200 crore and a self-certified innovation claim (https://www.startupindia.gov.in/content/sih/en/startupgov/startup_recognition_page.html). SISFS requires incorporation ≤2 years before applying, ≥51% Indian promoter shareholding and ≤₹10 lakh prior government support, and the ISMC scores eight criteria — market need, feasibility, potential impact, novelty/IP, team strength, fund-utilisation and related (https://www.startupindia.gov.in/content/dam/invest-india/Templates/public/Guidelines%20for%20Startup%20India%20Seed%20Fund%20Scheme.pdf, §3.1, §7.2). Backend language appears in none of them.
